lf-suggestion.description: One proposed change to content the user has already seen, decided in place. lf-old holds the current markup verbatim, lf-new the proposal: both slots replace, lf-new alone inserts, lf-old alone deletes. A widget-state change has no separate patch shape: put the complete old and new widget markup in those slots when one is genuinely needed. Pending, the old reads struck and the new tinted, with accept/reject controls in the page margin; deciding folds the retired half away and reaches the agent as an `accept` or `reject` action whose outcome survives later revisions. Deciding leaves visible Accepted or Rejected receipt text beside an Undo Button while the gesture can still be withdrawn. Undo or `z` takes back that named decision: the log keeps the decision and its withdrawal, and the change comes back pending — the runtime rebuilds it from the markup this version wrote, there being no value “undecided” for any verb to state. `resolves` names the comment whose thread this change answers — accepting resolves that thread too. Suggestions don't nest, and a reply can't carry one (reply markup is frozen in the log, so no version could settle it). Fresh content — a new section, the first version — is written straight instead, and a block the user is to write in their own words is a lf-draft: theirs to rewrite, not the agent's to propose. The user can also just comment on a pending suggestion rather than decide it. An undecided one can also be taken back: a later version drops the wrapper and everything inside lf-new with it, since withdrawing it leaves the page where a reject would (x-withdrawn-as). It can't keep the proposal as settled prose, and it can't drop what lf-old wraps — losing that is the user's own accept to give. An undecided one is a standing decision (see $awaits) — counted in the banner, stepped to by `a`/`A`, and the one kind a single press answers wholesale, which is the banner's Accept all.
lf-suggestion.x-example:
Refill rules for the season:

Refill every feeder each morning.

Refill a feeder when its camera shows it half-empty.

lf-old.description: The markup a suggestion would replace or delete, verbatim — ids and all, which live here while the suggestion is pending. Omitted when the suggestion only inserts. Accepting the suggestion retires this slot: its words leave the page's reading, so nothing can anchor on them after.

lf-new.description: The markup a suggestion proposes. Omitted when the suggestion only deletes. Rejecting the suggestion retires this slot: its words leave the page's reading, so nothing can anchor on them after.

$languages.description: The languages this page's layer can color, and what a filename means. `names` is the whole vocabulary: what an author may declare, what the lint refuses a word outside, and what the highlight and pierre bundles in scripts/vendor.py are built from. It is a property of the page rather than of any widget, which is why it lives here and not under the schema of whichever tag happens to take a `language` — a widget declares that one of its attributes names a language (x-language) and the lint reads the list from here, so a second tag taking one costs a declaration and no new reader. `paths` is the half nobody writes: the one place a language is derived rather than declared, because a unified diff spans files and so has no attribute to carry one. An extension is the diff's own statement about what a file holds, which is a declaration like any other; an extension absent here leaves that file plain.
$languages.why-diff-is-not-a-path: `diff` is in `names` and deliberately not in `paths`: a .patch inside a diff would be colored by the diff grammar, whose addition and deletion ink is the same statement the widget's own tints already make — said twice, in two channels, about the same line.

$data.description: Replaceable external or derived values supplied to widgets. A named contract declares the meaning and JSON Schema of a value; each widget declares its typed inputs, while page and thread markup binds those inputs to concrete source ids. One source id keeps one contract for the page's lifetime. `leaf data set` validates the complete value before it can reach a page. Source values remain outside authored versions and the event log. Modules subscribe with `watchData` and render readable records through `projectData`.

$events.description: The event contract this layer's runtime and CLI speak. Each kind carries a closed `record` schema for the complete event read from the log. A `browser` schema opts that kind into POST /api/event and adds the browser writer's assertions; a record contract alone opens no browser door. `page init` checks the existing log against the incoming record schemas before it re-vendors, so a recorded event never becomes unreadable. Kind contracts replace whole when layers merge: a half-old, half-new schema is no layer's statement. A `pickup` is the page-owned durable transport fact that named reader events reached their next consumer; it is never a claim that work has begun. A `comment` or `reply` carrying `token` instead of `text` is a reaction — one word from $reactions, aimed where the comment's anchor or the reply's parent points, or with neither at the page whole. It starts as a mark rather than a conversation: no thread opens until someone replies to it, `resolve` on it is the floor after which it stops painting, and while nothing has answered it the reader takes it back with an ordinary `undo` naming it.

$keys.description: What each x- key an entry may declare means, one member per key. The keys are the layer's and the lint closes the set, so a layer overriding a member here documents its own reading of that key and declares no new one; a member for a key the lint doesn't admit, or a key with no member, refuses the registry. Authors query this entry beside widget entries, and the site's table of keys is generated from it, so an author, the lint and the documentation read one thing.
$keys.x-decision: What x-decision declares: an instance is the complete reading and arrival region for exactly one non-quoted nested local Decision declared by x-awaits or x-request.decision. The region begins with one direct heading, then carries any context and evidence the reader needs before the control; the nested widget still owns the answer and its fold or Request lifecycle. The banner, Asks tray, `a`/`A` ask walk, standing ring, and `page state` name the region while action eligibility, replay, and Request projection name the nested widget. An arrival focuses that widget's answering control but scrolls to the region's start. `version check` requires the leading heading and one non-quoted nested Decision source so the two identities cannot be ambiguous.
$keys.x-awaits: What x-awaits declares: a tag either originates a standing Decision for the reader or, with `rollup: true`, aggregates descendant Decisions through a nested plan. A local Decision always names the x-state verbs that answer it. A roll-up owner can expose and gate on descendant Decisions without entering the Asks list itself. The banner's count, the `a`/`A` ask walk that steps asks, the `?` overlay's row, and conditional x-state actions are readings of one projection, so nothing names a tag and a new widget joins by declaring. Quoted material decides nothing — an exhibited Decision is a mention (x-exhibit). `region` says the widget supplies the answer control but not its own title: every matching local Decision must stand inside an x-decision, whose direct heading owns the question's reading and arrival. A widget that also declares x-conversation puts a box under its own Decision, and a conversation standing in that box takes the Decision off the reader's list for as long as it waits on the agent — whoever opened it. That is not an answer: the widget's state is untouched, so a version still has to record what the words settled, and an action's `requires` reads the Decision as open. An ordinary reply or resolve hands the conversation back. A version-response conversation takes no reply; only authored state in a later version that answers an originating open Decision, or changes its declared answer when the Decision was already answered, unlocks the agent's resolve. Reader actions in the log do not substitute for that version. A widget inside a thread presents a Decision like one on the page, with one bound set by frozen thread markup: the thread's own reply box is already that seat, so only an action can answer it there. `when` selects Decision instances, `answers` names exactly the x-state verbs that settle one, `rollup` carries the logical OR of descendant Decisions, `until` can require a distinct completion verb for a matching thread Decision, and `all` names a blanket answer offered by the banner.
$keys.x-conversation: The module places a conversationBox in each page instance matching authored, static `when` attributes (an attribute written by an x-state or x-report value record cannot drive this predicate). It projects exact-section threads textually from the whole log; Threads keeps the complete interactive view. Thread markup and quoted material take no second view. Where the widget also originates a local x-awaits Decision, the seat is where the reader deals with it in words: the Decision leaves their list while that conversation waits on the agent, rather than being counted a second time under a box they have already used. It is not an answer — the widget's own state is untouched, so its controls still work and an action's `requires` still reads the Decision as open. A conversation with `response: {kind: version, verb: <answer>}` carries that declaration on its root comment, has no inline reply control, and refuses `leaf reply`: the agent either incorporates it in a later version or opens a separate thread when that revision depends on the reader. To unlock resolve, authored state in the later version must answer an originating open Decision, or change the named answer's authored record when the Decision was already answered. Reader actions in the log do not substitute for that version. The named verb must be one of x-awaits' answers with an attribute or value record, so the resolve gate can compare the originating and current versions without naming a widget. A `hold` comment is such a conversation like any other. `hold` labels a stronger send route whose comment carries `holds` naming this widget: that route remains available after ordinary roots, the unresolved held thread is the hold, resolution releases it, and undoing resolution restores it atomically. Dropping the widget drops only the inline view.
$keys.x-content: The content model: `prose` (children are the author's markup), `items` (children are this widget's own item elements and nothing else), `data` (one <pre> holding text in the notation the description names, < > escaped — <pre> because it is the only thing in HTML that says whitespace is load-bearing without a stylesheet to read), or `none`. Required.
$keys.x-data: The widget's named external-data inputs. Each input names a `$data.contracts` contract and the declared canonical string attribute whose authored value is this page's source id. An optional `snapshot` names a declared positive-decimal attribute that selects an immutable source snapshot; without it the input follows the current value. An optional source attribute leaves that input absent; `watchData` delivers null. Several widgets may bind the same source to the same contract. Across immutable versions and widgets frozen into threads, one source cannot mean two contracts; use a new source id for a new meaning. A module subscribes by widget and input name, never by a package-owned source name.
$keys.x-example: Authored markup exhibiting the widget, valid against the merged registry: an agent reads it with the widget entry, writes from it, and the lint refuses one that does not validate.
$keys.x-exhibit: The element quotes what it holds rather than speaking it — a mention, not a use: interactive widgets inside take no input (a choose group no clicks, a board no drags, a suggestion no decision), and a decision inside it counts for nothing. A module asks `quoted(el)` before wiring any input, and the theme's affordance rules — the hand, the lift, the joined shape — stand down inside it on their own.
$keys.x-guidance: Audience-specific authoring or operating guidance owned by this widget. `page guidance` composes it with data-contract guidance and package-wide guidance, so instructions travel with the contribution they explain rather than with whichever package happened to distribute it.
$keys.x-inline: The element is set among the words around it, so the render gate holds its box to no width of its own and the rule that a block widget stands in a block slot passes over it.
$keys.x-language: The attribute that names a code language, held to `$languages.names` — the one list this page colors from — so a second tag taking a language costs a declaration and no new reader.
$keys.x-lines: Attributes holding 1-based line references into the nearest data body — the element's own <pre>, or its holder's (a note's `at` names a line of its code block) — which `version check` refuses outside the body.
$keys.x-measured: A scalar in authored content pinned to one x-data input at an aware instant. `input` names the widget's data input and `at` names its required date-time attribute. The authored words remain frozen with the version; when that source's stored `updated` instant moves past `at`, `version check` advises that the measurement is stale and `page state` reports the same debt. The declaration compares runs, not age: a source that never updates creates no warning.
$keys.x-paints: Attributes the theme renders as paint alone — for example, a status marker's tint or an event's kind. The runtime speaks each to a reader listening (the value, or a flag attribute's own name), silently on screen and out of every selection, so a fact stated in ink is not silent to whoever cannot see it.
$keys.x-parent: The widgets an instance may be a direct child of — an item's holder — and, read the other way, what a container is made of: a gesture a container takes on its whole box stops at what it holds, and this is where it reads which children are its own rather than things it merely contains.
$keys.x-refers: A map from attributes whose values name another element to their target contracts. An empty contract accepts any element id (an option's `for`). A typed contract names a shared registry map with `via` and an equality predicate with `where`; `version check` then requires both an existing id and a target tag whose declaration in that package-owned map matches the predicate. This lets a package distinguish a goal, worker, or evidence reference without Leaf knowing those roles or tags. The runtime renders every valid value as a reference the reader can follow.
$keys.x-report: What x-report declares, once per widget with an agent channel: report verbs a worker folds onto the page through `leaf report`, each with a detail schema (the payload half of the log's forever-contract, exactly as x-state's), a semantic facet, a fold unit, and a required record form drawn from $state's vocabulary minus `body`. An optional `update` names the required non-empty string detail field that is the report's short human-readable news; naming it lets the canonical update feed expose those words without guessing from a widget, verb, or field name. The owning widget instance, unit, and facet together name one independently standing fact; verbs on the same tag and facet share their unit and record form, and an action outranks a report at that coordinate. A report moves declared state only, never the page's words, which is what keeps the passage reading untouched by it. The runtime paints a standing report live (data-lf-reported); it is provisional news, standing only until a version answers it. How a version answers a standing report is $report's.
$keys.x-request: One-shot operations the reader asks the external host to perform. `offers` maps each direct child widget tag to its required string-enum verb attribute, deriving the commands a particular holder presents; every live holder must carry at least one such direct offer and may offer each verb only once. `verbs` declares every command's complete detail schema. Optional `bind` maps required string detail fields to required immutable string attributes on this widget, so a crafted request cannot retarget the operation. `decision: true` makes the ready lifecycle a reader decision: acceptance hands the turn to the host, pending and completed leave the reader's list, and failure returns it. `region: true` says the holder supplies the commands but not its own question title, so every instance stands inside an x-decision whose leading direct heading owns the reading and arrival. A page holder has one lifecycle per revision; a holder in frozen thread markup has one for that document's whole lifetime. Pending excludes another request, failure reopens it, and success completes it. Each request is durable and not undoable because the host may already have acted. `leaf receipt` appends exactly one linked `succeeded` or `failed` outcome, and `watchRequestLifecycle` supplies the holder's server-projected request seat, exact request/receipt attempts, latest attempt, and ready/pending/completed phase to its package module. Leaf transports and validates the protocol but does not interpret verbs or execute them; package-owned guidance tells the host what each verb means, and external data carries replaceable evidence produced by it.
$keys.x-retired-when: On a slot: the holder's action outcome that takes this element off the page (a suggestion's `lf-old` under `accept`). Requires x-parent. Every outcome named by one holder's slots belongs to the same facet, so only one settlement can stand. The layer renders the settlement whole, following the log's standing state both ways — reconciliation paints data-lf-state="<outcome>" on the holder and data-lf-retired on the slots that outcome retires, takes both off when a later widget-unit verb on that facet displaces the decision in the fold, and one theme rule hides the marked slots — so no module owes any of it, though one may paint the same sooner as its own gesture (renderRetired). The file's reading takes the fact from the log, and `version check` licenses dropping the slot's ids on it; `version check --render` reports a settled slot still showing words, or a mark the log never decided.
$keys.x-says: Attributes whose values the reader sees as words, and where each renders. `after` goes inside the element's own content, ahead of the apparatus that ends it, so a word does not land on the far side of a control that closes the row. `before` goes at the element's start, ahead of chrome as well: leading chrome is not something the words stand beside, it is a module speaking for the whole element, so an element's opening words go above it; where an entry declares two at that edge they render in the order the entry lists them. The runtime writes them as selectable text the user can quote and comment on, where `content: attr()` would paint glyphs into no text node.
$keys.x-shadow: The module renders the page's words into an open shadow tree, which the passage walk, the selection capture and every question asked by id cross; a shadow root on a host whose entry lacks it is a render-gate finding.
$keys.x-state: What x-state declares, once per widget with an action channel: each verb's detail schema (the payload half of the log's forever-contract), its semantic facet, fold unit, optional current-state `requires`, optional generated-child `creates`, and the record form its state takes in markup. The owning widget instance, unit, and facet together name one independently standing fact: verbs on the same tag and facet share their unit and record form, competing verbs there supersede one another, and distinct facets coexist. Every applyAction is absolute, so the user's standing state is the last surviving action per coordinate, and one declaration drives the POST and re-vendor contract gates, `version check`'s state gate (a version whose markup actively contradicts the fold without `restated` is refused; writing the folded state is honoring; re-emitting the previous version's state is blessed silence), construction-linked inspection, the runtime's reader-origin mark, and the version diff's state half. The browser uses `requires` for its controls and common send door; POST interprets the same prerequisite against the authoritative fold under the append lock. One detail field name is reserved across every verb: `resolves` means the comment thread this action answers, thread settlement reads it on any action, and the lint holds a verb declaring the name to a plain string on a widget-absolute unit — a thread is answered by the decision, and a decision is a widget instance ($awaits). Because thread history can outlive its markup, every action verb on a resolves-bearing tag shares one answer facet. A report verb spelling the name is refused outright: settlement reads actions, so the field there would declare an answer nothing gives. What settles the thread is the widget's standing answer rather than the fact an answer was once given, so an answer that a later action at that coordinate supersedes, or that a `restated` takes back, leaves the thread open again. The facet, unit, requires, creates, and record forms are $state's.
$keys.x-thread-surface: The upgraded widget can seat canonical Thread views beside exact projected datums. Its module registers one adapter through registerThreadSurface; the adapter owns only outlet geometry and visibility, while Leaf owns Thread rendering, reply and reaction state, settlement, focus, receipts, and living-margin fallback. Returning an outlet claims that thread locally for the current reconciliation; unloaded, filtered, collapsed, outdated, or otherwise undisplayable datums return no outlet and remain in the global Threads index plus the ordinary fallback.
$keys.x-tone: The attribute that names one of the layer's semantic tints, held to `$tones.names`, which the theme has a rule for.
$keys.x-upgrade: A module at widgets/<tag>.js enhances the element in the browser, imported where a page's markup carries the tag rather than for the whole layer. `page init` refuses a layer declaring it with no module beside it, and the render gate a module that defines no element for a widget the page contains. Required.
$keys.x-verbatim: An upgraded element whose body reaches the reader as its own words — the module leaves it in place — which is what makes it quotable; a body without it is source the widget renders (a diagram's notation). The render gate refuses an x-verbatim whose rendered words differ from the file's.
$keys.x-visual: How a rendered picture exposes stable Comment targets. `whole` anchors the picture on the authored widget. `{parts: ATTR}` lets its module map tokens from ATTR to stable generated parts through `lfVisualPartAt(target)` and `lfVisualPart(part)`, which returns `{element, label}`. The returned element is the semantic target for marks, travel, and aim. Marks and aim follow a returned SVG element's painted primitives; other elements use the shown box. Targeting a mapped part stores its token as `anchor.visual` while the widget remains the semantic seat. A missing token or provider detaches on replay rather than widening to the whole picture. The render gate requires both provider methods on every matching instance.
$keys.x-wide: The width model, for evidence set to its content rather than to the measure prose is read at: `box` (the widget lays its content out into whatever width it is given, a board's columns, so it stands at the one width the whole vocabulary shares) or `drawing` (the widget renders one thing drawn at a size of its own, a diagram's graph, so its box is the clip around it — the room the page has, with the drawing as near the column's axis as the claimed margins allow, and scrolling where even the room is short). A drawing declares no `x-says`: that box is laid out as a row holding what was drawn, so a word the layer writes into it would stand beside the drawing rather than over it, and the registry refuses the pair. Nothing is authored for it and no page asks: the theme grows the element out of the column into whichever margins are free. A margin holding something of the page's gives nothing where it holds it, and only there: an exhibit level with a note drops below it and then takes the whole width; one level with a suggestion's controls keeps its place and declines their side, a positioned row being nothing an exhibit can drop below; and one that nothing reaches keeps its place and grows both ways.
$keys.x-withdrawn-as: On a holder with retirable slots: the outcome an undecided instance stands as when a later version takes it back unanswered — a withdrawn suggestion leaves the page where a `reject` would — which is what lets that version drop the ids inside the slots the outcome retires. Hedged, because there the author asserts a state the user never gave: only whole, and never while a thread is anchored in it.
$keys.x-word: What x-word declares: this tag's own word for what it is comes from its module, which answers `lfWord()` on the element, rather than from the tag's name. Almost no widget declares it, and none needs to while one tag is one kind of thing: a name away from the page is then the tag with its prefix dropped. It is wrong where a tag holds several kinds. Every shape of lf-suggestion came out as "suggestion", so a row on the decisions tray named a deletion by the words it proposed to remove and read exactly like the insertion above it. The word is asked for wherever the page names an element away from itself — a tray row, a comment's anchor label — and an element that has not upgraded yet, or answers nothing, falls back to the tag.
$keys.x-work: Where this widget can admit `leaf status --on` without a pending reader move: `content` names a block prose seat; `conversation` names the widget's declared x-conversation box and therefore inherits that box's own predicate. An optional `when` narrows the instances that may admit work under their replayed attributes. Once admitted, a page-widget claim appears at the page edge through its Target Button even if a later layer changes x-work. The declaration is permission for runtime chrome, not a consequence of x-content: prose may itself be a holder gesture or sit in a hidden panel.

$state.facet: A stable HTML-name identifying one independently standing fact within this tag. Together with the owning widget instance and unit it is the fold coordinate. Verbs on the same facet share one unit and an identical record form (or are all recordless); facet names are semantic and local to the tag, not a closed vocabulary.
$state.unit: "widget" for a verb absolute across the group (choose toggles every sibling), or the detail field naming the element the verb is absolute per (move's "card").
$state.requires: An optional prerequisite over the standing-decision projection x-awaits already defines. `target` is `self` or the widget's declared `parent`; `awaiting` says whether that decision must still be open. Open means unanswered, not on the reader's list: a conversation standing in the widget's x-conversation seat takes the decision off that list without answering it, and a gate reading the list instead would refuse the reader's pick for their having remarked on the question. A module calls `actionAvailable(widget, verb)` to paint and guard the exact gesture; `sendAction` and POST repeat the declaration, with POST reading the authoritative log under the append lock. Omit it for an action available in every state.
$state.creates: An optional generated-child contract `{field, child}` on an x-state verb. `field` names an optional detail map from canonical element ids to non-empty prose; `child` names the exact prose tag those ids become as direct children of the sender. The browser stores the sorted keys in the action's `generated` snapshot, which registry-free historical folds use for liveness. POST requires exact agreement, and re-vendoring preserves the declaration for every recorded action.
$state.record: How the state reads in markup: {kind: "attribute", attr, value} — every element inside the unit carrying attr, sorted, vs the ids the detail field `value` lists, which is why that field is an array however many the widget allows at once; {kind: "position", within, value, order} — the enclosing `within` element, compared at that granularity (indexes compose across cards, so column is the whole comparison) while `order` names the integer detail field counting the unit's siblings, which is what a reader stating a placement rather than comparing one needs; {kind: "body", value} — the unit's own words; {kind: "value", attr, value} — the unit's own attr holding one scalar, whose detail field carries the attribute's own schema so the log's contract and the markup's cannot drift. Within one tag and unit, body and position are each one physical slot; value slots are keyed by their host attr, and attribute-set slots by their descendant attr. Distinct facets cannot claim the same slot. A record is also how a gesture is taken back cheaply: the runtime reads the version's authored state through it before replay touches the page, so `z` can state what stood before the first action at a coordinate and the page moves rather than being rebuilt. A verb with no record (accept/reject) folds for the runtime's reader-origin mark and is taken back the other way — the widget rebuilt from the version's own markup, since “undecided” is a value no verb carries — and retirement stays retirable_ids' business.

$report.answering: Explicit, by typed id. `version stamp` puts a `report` target in the note's `settles` relation for every standing report the stamped revision answered: one whose recorded state the markup writes is absorbed, and one on an element marked `overruled` is overruled — the why belongs in the note's text. Replay stops a settled report at that revision. Silence — markup unchanged — settles nothing, so the report keeps painting. `version check` refuses the third thing, markup that contradicts a standing report it never settles, and refuses an `overruled` with nothing to overrule, exactly as the reviewer gate polices `restated`.
$report.overruled: A boolean attribute on the reported element, declared by every x-report widget: this revision keeps its own state over the standing report. It belongs to the revision whose stamp does the overruling — stamping records the answer on the note, so later revisions leave it off.
$report.updates: Reports and replace-in-place work claims share one derived update feed in log-causal order. Every entry has a typed target (`widget` or `thread`), source (`report` or `claim`), action, structured detail, optional declared text, speaker, timestamp, and one closed disposition: `effective` contributes to current state on its semantic coordinate, `standing` still awaits source-specific settlement but is presently outranked, and `settled` has been answered by that authority. A claim also carries `log_floor`, the log sequence it followed, so an agent reply after that floor or a resolution settles it without comparing wall clocks; a version note settles a report by id. The stores stay different because those authorities are different; consumers do not read either store directly.
$report.wakes: A report joins the watcher's batch: `leaf wait` prints it beside user events, the same `ack` acknowledges it, and idling is refused over one nobody read. The reader's banner counts none of this — a report is news the agent owes the page, not something the reader owes an answer.

$settlement.description: The typed `settles` relation on a version note ends provisional agent facts. Each target is `{kind, id}` so independently allocated id namespaces cannot collide and adding a kind does not add another parallel note field. The relation is explicit and durable: chronology alone ends nothing, and a later note need not repeat a settlement.
$settlement.report: The id is a report event. Stamping derives these targets from reported state the source absorbs or explicitly overrules.
$settlement.work: The id is a page-widget work subject. `version stamp --completes` accepts only standing work claimed before that revision and writes this target; it also licenses the revision to remove the subject's page target.
$settlement.why-restated-is-separate: `restated` is not a settlement. It retracts a reader decision because authored words or state invalidated what the decision rested on, while `settles` completes provisional information supplied by the agent. Conflating them would make ending work look like taking back the reader's action.

$awaits.when: The attribute condition that makes a local instance a Decision: each attribute maps to the values that require a decision, a flag attribute's values being true and false. Every named condition must match. A group takes picks only with `choose` and stops requiring a decision once it is `settled`. An entry with no `when` is a Decision on every instance, which is what a pending suggestion is.
$awaits.answers: The x-state verbs that answer this local Decision. Every local x-awaits declaration names at least one, so each Decision has a durable completion gesture. A completion verb cannot require its own awaiting value, or an aggregate parent's awaiting value, to be false: either circular prerequisite would make the gesture unavailable exactly while it is needed. Naming answer verbs also keeps orthogonal actions from accidentally closing the Decision. An attribute or scalar value record reads through authored markup as well as the fold, so a version that honors an answer remains answered and a cleared value opens the Decision again; every other named verb answers through its own standing action. A conversation in the widget's own seat (x-conversation) is not an answer; it only takes the Decision off the reader's list while the next word there is the agent's.
$awaits.rollup: True makes the instance an aggregate-only owner in a nested plan projection. Its awaiting value is the logical OR of its nearest local Decisions and child roll-ups. The owner never originates or surfaces a Decision, but carries that aggregate for plan summaries and parent action prerequisites. The visible Decisions are the open local descendants. Descendants join by x-awaits, never by tag.
$awaits.until: The verb that closes a thread Decision a record can't: an instance matching `until.when` stays open, whatever its record state, until the reader has posted `until.verb` on it. It exists for the set-valued question — a `multiple` group's toggles each reach the agent live, so only the reader can say the set is whole, and the widget renders the press that says it (lf-options' Done). Consulted only in the thread layer: on the page the record answers as ever, versions can honor and retire, and no submit stands between a pick and the agent.
$awaits.all: The verb a blanket yes takes, where one banner control can answer every Decision of this kind at once (`Accept all (3)`). The widget exposes a method of that name answering one instance, so the control records each decision separately rather than one blanket consent. Leave it off and the Decision is answered where the reader is, one at a time.

$restated.description: A boolean attribute saying this revision has rewritten words the user already decided on, so what they decided no longer applies and they are being asked again. It goes on the element the decision rests on — a lf-draft or lf-suggestion, or the lf-card or lf-option inside a board or group — and retracts every action that named it: a move names one card, so a rewritten card drops that card's moves, leaving the rest of the board arranged as the user left it; a pick names every option chosen at once, so a rewritten option takes back the whole answer it was part of.
$restated.why: A move, pick, edit or accept is recorded in the log against the revision it was made on, and the page reconciles every standing action onto every later revision. A decision therefore survives a new save on its own — you never carry one into the next revision's markup, and re-emitting a widget as you first wrote it does not undo it. The cost is that your markup cannot quietly overrule them either, which is what this attribute is for.
$restated.when: Only where a later revision has to change what the user decided about: an error you found in a draft they rewrote, a picked option whose prose was wrong. Write the new words, mark that element, and say why in the next stamp's note — to the user this reads as a decision undone, and the note is where a version explains itself. `version check` refuses a revision that changes those words without it and a `restated` that retracts nothing, so it can be neither forgotten nor spent as a reflex; when it names the wrong element, the error says which one it wanted.
$restated.once: It belongs to the one revision that does the rewriting. Stamping records the retraction in the log, so it holds for good — later revisions leave the attribute off, and `version check` refuses one that repeats it.
$restated.example: Adds --dry-run to every mutating command. It defaults on for `purge`.

$series.description: The categorical steps this layer paints a chart's series in, and how many of them there are. It is a property of the page rather than of any widget: the colours are --series-1 through --series-N in the theme, so a project that restates the palette with a step more says so once, here and beside the tokens, and every consumer reads the same number. `steps` is what a chart refuses a series past — two series in one colour is worse than a drawing that says it will not draw — and what the palette's own check counts the tokens against. The list is short on purpose: past five, the steps stop clearing the separation a reader with colour-vision deficiency needs, and a sixth is a chart that lies to some readers and to no others.

$reactions.description: The reaction vocabulary: the one-press words a reader can put on a passage, an element, a message in a thread, or the page whole, each recorded as a `comment` or `reply` carrying `token` in place of `text` ($events). The kernel declares the namespace and no word; the default package ships the working set, and any layer — a project's .leaf/, the user's ~/.config/leaf/ — reshapes it merge-patch style: an entry under a token's name replaces that token, a new name adds one, `null` removes one. Core never names a token. Everything a consumer needs rides the entry: `glyph` is the mark the page paints for it — one or two characters — in the margin, in the reaction list, and on a thread's strip; `means` is the sentence `leaf wait` prints beside the event, so a custom token is self-describing to whichever agent reads it; `settles`, where true, says a reaction of this kind standing on the latest agent message of a thread takes that thread out of "waiting on you" — a projection rule the panel reads, never a second event. POST refuses a token outside the merged set, the way $languages gates a language name. Tokens stand independently on one target; reaction lists and their optional digit accelerators follow this declared order, so a digit survives any layer's renaming without changing a pill's label.

$tones.description: The semantic tints this layer paints, and the whole vocabulary an author may declare: what the lint refuses a word outside, and what the theme has a rule for. It is a property of the page rather than of any widget, which is why it lives here and not under the schema of whichever tag happens to take a `tone` — a widget declares that one of its attributes names one (x-tone) and the lint reads the list from here, so a second tag taking a tone costs a declaration and no new reader. The list is short on purpose: a page that can paint anything paints nothing, and three is what the palette already answers for. Which facts earn a tint is never the theme's to decide — `ok` on one page's chip and `danger` on another's may be the same word, because the author is the only one who knows whether the answer is good news.

$idioms.description: Recurring shapes the theme styles directly — no registry entry, no JS. Plain semantic HTML gets the theme's voice for free; these classes cover what HTML lacks an element for. Each key is the CSS selector the shape is written as, and the example beside it is that markup. A layer adds one by declaring it here and styling it in its theme.css; members merge across layers, so the declaration joins this catalog rather than replacing it.

.eyebrow.description: A small-caps label above a heading.

.lede.description: The opening paragraph, set slightly larger.
.lede.example: One paragraph saying what this page decides.

.callout.description: An aside set off from the prose — a tinted field with a hairline border. For something the reader must not miss; a note they lose nothing by skipping goes in the margin (aside.sidenote).
.callout.example: <aside class="callout" id="rollback-note">Rollback is one flag flip; the backfill is idempotent.</aside>

aside.sidebar.description: Page-level supporting material in the left margin: local navigation, a compact legend, or stable reference facts that remain useful while the reader moves through a long page. Use one, as a direct child of main near the page's opening, rather than beside the one paragraph it concerns; that local annotation is an aside.sidenote. On a roomy live screen the first such child sits left of the prose and sticks beneath Leaf's banner; a fine-pointer lf-toc can use that margin as a fixed reading map instead. Where the page's own box has no room for the strip — a narrow window, a second margin resident, or a thread panel or decisions tray taking part of a middling one — and on paper or in a standalone copy, the sidebar returns to ordinary flow where it was authored. An accidental second sidebar also stays in flow instead of occupying the first. Keep the contents compact enough to scan in about 240px. The wrapper supplies placement, not a visual panel, so what it holds keeps its own voice; an lf-toc is the usual navigation occupant but the idiom is not coupled to that widget. Its content remains part of the page and may be selected or commented on unless the occupant itself declares apparatus.
aside.sidebar.example:
On this page
  1. Prepare
  2. Move

aside.sidenote.description: A note in the page's right margin: a caveat, a provenance, a figure the sentence had no room for. It is read where it stands and skipped at no cost, where a .callout sits in the column the reader is reading down and a <details> asks for a click. Write it immediately before the paragraph, list or block it annotates, and it comes out level with that block's first line; before a heading it sits above the heading instead, a heading carrying more room over it than the block before it leaves. A second note written soon after the first stacks under it, so a long note pushes the next one down the margin and away from its own block. It reaches the margin through any box that doesn't clip — a section, a tab panel, a disclosure; written inside one that does, a choose group or a board or a table, it is drawn nowhere at all, and `version check --render` refuses the version rather than letting it ship. Where the page's box has no room for the strip — a narrow window, or the thread panel taking its side of a middling one — and on paper, it is a small indented block where it was written, so nothing it says rests on the margin being there. A suggestion's accept and reject controls hang in the same margin, level with the change they decide, and are drawn over a note that stands level with them: write the note a paragraph clear of a change if its first line has to be read. These are the page's own words, so the reader can select, quote and comment on one. A stable id lets Alt-click point at the whole note. The margin holds about fifty-six characters to the line; a note running past a few lines wants to be a paragraph in the column instead.
aside.sidenote.example:
Support runs "log out all devices" during account-takeover response, about twice a month.

Logout must revoke immediately, which rules out any store whose invalidation is eventually consistent.

.facts.description: A label/value grid for summary facts, as a definition list. Inside a card that stands for one alternative in a group, it docks right as a fixed-width rail instead, aligning each item's scalars down the group.

ol.steps.description: An ordered procedure with numbered markers.
ol.steps.example:
1. Backfill the new store.
  2. Verify counts, then flip reads.

table.description: Rows of one shape, compared column by column: ceilings per plan, runs per configuration. Columns take the width of what they hold, and a table wider than the measure wraps its cells or, failing that, scrolls inside itself — so nothing in one needs a width. An identifier — a test name, a path — is one word to the line breaker: in `<code>` it breaks inside its cell where it must, so a column of them takes a share of the measure beside the prose; bare, it holds its column to its own width and squeezes the rest to a word a line, and `version check --render` refuses a table that scrolls sideways with a cell in it wrapped. `<th scope="row">` names a row in the page's own voice; a bare `<th>` is a column heading, set in small caps as one. A `<caption>` above the rows says what the columns mean where the section's heading doesn't. Reach for a KPI widget when the numbers are a handful of headline figures rather than a grid, and a decision widget when the rows are alternatives the reader picks between.
table.example:
Ceilings per plan, and what each is counted against.
PlanA minuteCounted against
Free60the token
Team600the token

td.num.description: A cell holding a quantity, right-aligned so a column of them lines up on its last digit — the comparison a column of figures is there for. Say it on the column's heading cell too, or the heading hangs left of its own figures. Nothing is guessed from the text: "60" and "60 sessions" are the same shape and different things.

details.description: Evidence: a claim as the <summary>, its backing collapsed beneath. Native disclosure; find-in-page reaches the collapsed content.
details.example:
The parser drops the slash on self-closed custom tags 
document.querySelector("lf-metric").textContent
// → "rest of the paragraph"

pre > code[class*=\"language-\"].description: A literal the user can select and quote: a command to run, a config file, a snippet of output. Name the language to color it — one of $languages, the same list a widget's own language attribute is held to, and `version check` refuses one outside it. Leave the class off where the body isn't source; nothing is guessed from the text. Reach for an annotated code block instead when the block is a walkthrough: numbered lines, highlighted ranges, remarks anchored at a line.
